tagline.text: A white-sand beach on Romblon Island where a sandbar path opens at low tide

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Lonos, west of Romblon town, Romblon Island

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,500 (per person, local transport and meals only, excluding travel to the island)

children.text: Bonbon Beach lies about a 10-minute motorbike ride from Romblon town on Romblon Island. It is known for fine white sand, clear water and a long sandbar that leads to the uninhabited Bangug Island at low tide, and it was named to the World's 50 Best Beaches lists in 2024 and 2025.
Bonbon Beach is on Romblon Island, the main island of Romblon province. It belongs to Barangay Lonos in the municipality of Romblon and lies about
3–5 km

from the town center and the port. Sources give distances anywhere from 3 to 5 km, but several travel accounts agree that it is around 10 minutes away by tricycle or motorbike. It is close enough to the port that you can visit on the afternoon you arrive on the island.
The sandbar is what made the beach famous. A strip of sand runs out to sea and joins the uninhabited island of Bangug (also written Bang-og or Ban-Og), and it is described as about
2 km

long. At low tide the sandbar is almost fully exposed and you can walk across to the island, but at high tide the water rises to about waist level and parts of it are submerged. The same beach can look completely different depending on the hour. The Department of Tourism (DOT) and local media announced that Bonbon Beach made the 2024 World's 50 Best Beaches list, and it appeared again in 2025. One broadcast report placed it at No. 38 for 2025.

The atmosphere is that of a quiet, lightly developed stretch of sand. Wikipedia describes fine white sand and a gently sloping bottom free of seagrass and sharp stones, and travel blogs describe a simple beach with no resorts or commercial facilities. Those accounts date from around 2018, so basic facilities may have appeared since. Some sources say the land is privately owned while others call the beach public, so check entrance and parking arrangements on site. The water is clear, the waves are calm and it is easy to wade in, which makes it manageable for families with children.

Romblon is known as an island of marble, and many travelers build a day or two around Bonbon Beach. A typical plan combines Fort San Andres and Fort San Jose, the marble workshops, and the nearby Tiamban and Talipasak beaches, with a boat trip to Carabao Island if time allows. Getting here from Manila takes a full day by boat, so it does not suit a rushed itinerary, but it rewards anyone who wants a quiet rest. The fares and schedules below were checked in 2026 and change often, so confirm the latest information before you leave.

blocks.title: A sandbar that opens at low tide

children.text: A sandbar links the beach to Bangug Island, and you can walk across at low tide. The best time is when the water is at its lowest. The sandbar is exposed for a long stretch with sea on both sides, which makes it great for photos. Check that day's tide table before you go.

This large rocky island at the end of the sandbar is uninhabited. If you walk up onto it, the view back toward the beach looks different from the other side. You must return before the water rises, so set a turnaround time and stick to it.
Fine white sand and a gently sloping bottom with little seagrass make it pleasant for walking barefoot or playing in shallow water. The sea is calm and fairly clear.
Travel accounts recommend sunrise and sunset for the best photos and say mornings are quieter. If you stay in Romblon town, you can rent a motorbike and head out before sunrise.

Its place on the World's 50 Best Beaches lists in 2024 and 2025 has brought a noticeable rise in domestic and foreign visitors. Rankings change every year, so check recent reports. Because it is now well known, it can be busier on weekends and holidays.
No large resort has been built here, so it remains a simple beach. Do not expect parasols or big restaurants. Bring water and snacks, and take your trash with you.
Tiamban Beach, Dolphin Beach and Talipasak (San Pedro) Beach are close to Romblon town. Rather than seeing just one, you can link two or three by motorbike for a full day.

Fort San Andres and Fort San Jose on the hill behind the port, St. Joseph's Cathedral and the marble streets are within walking distance, so you can combine the beach and the town in one day. Fort San Andres sits on a hill overlooking the port and town, so the view at dusk is good, and Wikipedia lists it as a National Cultural Treasure.

items.title: Half-day plan
items.subtitle: A sandbar walk timed to the tide

children.text: Head to Bonbon Beach from your lodging by tricycle or rented motorbike. Check the low-tide time the night before.
Park and walk about
to the beach. Take photos on the quiet morning sand.
Time it with the low tide and walk the sandbar toward Bangug Island. Decide when you will turn back.
Return to the beach to swim and relax. There is little shade, so use a hat and sunscreen.
Head back to Romblon town for lunch. In the afternoon you can continue to the forts or the cathedral.
Tides differ every day, so fit your plans around the tide. Head back as soon as the water begins to rise over the sandbar.

items.title: Full-day plan
items.subtitle: A tour of Romblon Island's beaches

children.text: Watch the sunrise at Bonbon Beach and walk across the sandbar.
Have breakfast in town, then visit Fort San Andres and Fort San Jose.
After lunch, stop by Tiamban or Talipasak Beach by motorbike for a swim.
Walk around the marble workshop area or St. Joseph's Cathedral.
Return to Bonbon Beach near sundown to watch the sunset.
Take a bus from PITX or elsewhere in Manila to Batangas Port (about ₱150–200).
From Batangas Port, check
Starlite Ferries’ service to Romblon Port
. Select Romblon Port in Romblon town to land on the same island as Bonbon Beach. The Odiongan terminal is on Tablas, a different island in the province.

Consider the Odiongan and San Agustin transfer only if the Romblon Port sailing does not suit your dates. The journey from Odiongan to San Agustin is by road. Confirm the San Agustin to Romblon Port sailing separately.

Ferry times and fares change with the season. Check announcements from operators such as Starlite Ferries and Montenegro Lines. One guide notes that some routes toward Sibuyan Island do not run every day.

Romblon Island has no scheduled airport. The nearest airport with air service is Tugdan Airport (TBH) on Tablas Island. Whether direct Manila flights operate, and at what price, varies by period, so check with the airline.
From Tugdan Airport, the journey to Romblon port continues overland and by boat and takes several hours.

Romblon has no sharply defined dry and wet season. Rain is generally heaviest from June to November, and January to May is closer to a dry season. Seas are calmest and skies clearest from February to May.

Within a single day, the low-tide window matters most. You can only walk the sandbar properly when the water is out, and sunrise and sunset are best for photos. In the rainy season, leave slack in your schedule because ferries may be cancelled.

Lodging is in Romblon town and along the coast. Travel blogs mention Lanas Beach Resort on the beachfront, Stone Creek House in the center and Sunrise Cove, a dive resort, among others. Names and rates change with the season, so check recent reviews on a booking site. There is generally no lodging at Bonbon Beach itself, so most people travel back and forth from town.

You will mostly eat at restaurants and the market in Romblon town. Many accounts say there are no large restaurants at the beach, so bring water, snacks and lunch. You can try grilled seafood and Filipino home cooking, and packing a lunch is convenient on days when you tour the island.
Romblon town is warm all year, with an average temperature of about

and annual rainfall reported at around 2,400 mm. If it rains, put off the sandbar walk and visit the forts and churches first, then head to the beach when the weather clears. There are no convenience stores near the beach, so buy water and snacks at your lodging in advance.
Check that day's low-tide time before you go, and cross the sandbar during the one to two hours before low tide.
Early morning is the quietest, and sunrise photos come out well.
There is little shade, so bring a hat, sunscreen and plenty of water.
If you rent a motorbike, it is easy to link other beaches such as Tiamban and Talipasak.
Take all your trash with you. There may be no trash cans on the beach.
Keep your phone and camera in a waterproof pouch in case the water rises suddenly on the sandbar.
Getting to the island takes a full day, so plan for at least two nights.

The sandbar is submerged to about waist depth when the tide comes in. Set a time to return from Bangug Island, and come back right away if the water begins to rise.
Tide times differ every day, so check the tide table and do not linger at the end of the sandbar.
Some sources say the beach is private land and others say it is public. Follow the signs and rules on site for access and fees.
There may be no lifeguards at the beach, so swim in shallow water and keep children close.
On days with typhoons or high waves, ferries can be cancelled and sea conditions can turn bad, so check the weather forecast.
